articles.title: Pioneering fossil hunter recognised with blue plaque
articles.summary: Dorothea Bate discovered the dwarf elephant and the myotragus, an extinct goat-like antelope.
articles.content:
A pioneering fossil hunter who was one of the first women to be employed by the Natural History Museum has been recognised with a national blue plaque.

Dorothea Bate, who died in 1951 aged 72, "transformed our understanding of prehistoric animals and ancient environments" through her research, Historic England said.

She has been recognised with a plaque at the Natural History Museum, in Tring, Hertfordshire, which notes in its inscription that the palaeontologist was the "Officer-in-Charge of this museum from 1948".

Bate was born in Carmarthen, Wales, in 1878 and developed a fascination with the natural world from an early age.

She moved with her family to rural Gloucestershire as a young woman and spent hours exploring the surrounding countryside and caves, collecting fossils.

She had little formal education, instead largely teaching herself, and in 1900 asked for work behind the scenes at the Natural History Museum in London.

Her determination impressed museum staff, earning her a position as an assistant and beginning an association with the institution that would last more than 50 years.

She published her first scientific paper, A Short Account Of A Bone Cave In The Carboniferous Limestone Of The Wye Valley, in 1901.

Bate went on to undertake expeditions across the Mediterranean, often travelling alone to remote caves in search of evidence of ancient life.

In Cyprus, she discovered a previously unknown species of dwarf elephant and in 1909, while in the Balearics, she discovered the myotragus - an extinct goat-like antelope.

She achieved more than 80 published scientific papers, despite spending most of her career without a permanent paid position.

In 2017, a blue plaque was dedicated to Bate at Napier House in Carmarthen where she was born.

articles.personality_title: Dorothea Bate honored with blue plaque for fossil discoveries
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Dorothea Bate was one of the first women to work at the Natural History Museum in London. She spent many years studying fossils and made important discoveries about ancient animals.

**What happened** – A blue plaque was put up at the Natural History Museum in Tring, Hertfordshire, to honor Bate. The plaque notes that she was once the Officer-in-Charge of the museum. Born in Wales in 1878, Bate taught herself about fossils and started working at the museum in 1900. She traveled alone to caves around the Mediterranean and found new species like a dwarf elephant and an extinct goat-like antelope called the myotragus.

**Impact** – Bate’s work changed how scientists understand prehistoric animals and environments. She wrote more than 80 scientific papers even though she didn’t have a permanent paid job for most of her life. Her recognition with a blue plaque helps people remember her important role in science and encourages more awareness of women’s contributions.

**What’s next step** – This plaque could inspire museums and schools to share more stories about women scientists like Bate. It may also lead to more public interest in fossils and history, encouraging young people to explore science.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Dorothea Bate’s fossil discoveries and dedication earned her lasting recognition, highlighting her key role in the history of science.
articles.personality_title_fr: Dorothea Bate honorée par une plaque bleue pour ses découvertes fossiles
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Dorothea Bate fut l'une des premières femmes à travailler au Muséum d'histoire naturelle de Londres. Elle a passé de nombreuses années à étudier des fossiles et a fait des découvertes importantes sur les animaux anciens.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Une plaque bleue a été installée au Muséum d'histoire naturelle de Tring, dans le Hertfordshire, pour honorer Bate. La plaque indique qu'elle fut responsable du musée. Née au Pays de Galles en 1878, Bate s'est autoformée aux fossiles et a commencé à travailler au musée en 1900. Elle a voyagé seule dans des grottes en Méditerranée et a découvert de nouvelles espèces comme un éléphant nain et une antilope éteinte appelée myotragus.

**Impact** – Le travail de Bate a changé la compréhension des scientifiques sur les animaux préhistoriques et leur environnement. Elle a écrit plus de 80 articles scientifiques même si elle n'a pas eu de poste payé permanent la plupart de sa vie. Sa reconnaissance par cette plaque bleue aide à se souvenir de son rôle important en science et à mieux connaître les contributions des femmes.

**Étape suivante** – Cette plaque pourrait encourager les musées et écoles à raconter davantage d'histoires sur des femmes scientifiques comme Bate. Cela pourrait aussi susciter plus d'intérêt public pour les fossiles et l'histoire, incitant les jeunes à explorer la science.

**Une phrase clé** – Les découvertes fossiles et la détermination de Dorothea Bate lui ont valu une reconnaissance durable, soulignant son rôle clé dans l'histoire des sciences.
articles.personality_title_es: Dorothea Bate reconocida con placa azul por sus descubrimientos fósiles
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Dorothea Bate fue una de las primeras mujeres en trabajar en el Museo de Historia Natural de Londres. Pasó muchos años estudiando fósiles y realizó importantes descubrimientos sobre animales antiguos.

**Qué pasó** – Se colocó una placa azul en el Museo de Historia Natural en Tring, Hertfordshire, para honrar a Bate. La placa señala que fue la encargada del museo. Nacida en Gales en 1878, Bate se enseñó a sí misma sobre fósiles y comenzó a trabajar en el museo en 1900. Viajó sola a cuevas en el Mediterráneo y descubrió nuevas especies como un elefante enano y un antílope extinto llamado myotragus.

**Impacto** – El trabajo de Bate cambió la forma en que los científicos entienden a los animales prehistóricos y su entorno. Escribió más de 80 artículos científicos aunque no tuvo un puesto fijo y pagado la mayor parte de su vida. Su reconocimiento con una placa azul ayuda a recordar su importante papel en la ciencia y a dar más visibilidad a las contribuciones de las mujeres.

**Próximo paso** – Esta placa podría inspirar a museos y escuelas a compartir más historias sobre mujeres científicas como Bate. También puede aumentar el interés público en los fósiles y la historia, motivando a los jóvenes a explorar la ciencia.

**Una frase para recordar** – Los descubrimientos fósiles y la dedicación de Dorothea Bate le valieron un reconocimiento duradero, destacando su papel clave en la historia de la ciencia.
